title: Happy Birthday!
bodyHtml:
The Ewe language is spoken principally in Ghana, Togo, and Benin. Names in Ewe are often connected to the day on which a person was born. (Not all Ewe names are related to date of birth, but all the names used in this problem are.) Below are some dates along with one possible name for a child born on each date. For your convenience, we have also provided calendars for January 2024 and February 2024 below. All dates in this problem are from 2024. “ɔ” is a vowel sound a little like the “aw” in “paw”.

January 7Kɔsi (male child)January 27Kwami (male child)
January 9Kɔbla (male child)February 6Abla (female child)
January 11Yawa (female child)February 11Akosua (female child)
January 14Kwasi (male child)February 13Kwamla (male child)
January 15Kɔdzo (male child)February 22Yao (male child)
January 20Ami (female child)February 26Adzoa (female child)
January 24Aku (female child)

questions.partPrompt: Indicate whether each name below would typically be a female name or a male name. Write F for female or M for male.
Match each date below to a name that could be given to a child born on that day. Choose from: (a) Afua, (b) Kɔku, (c) Yao, (d) Adzoa, (e) Kɔmi, (f) Abla. Each name is used exactly once.
On which day could a child named Kofi have been born? Write the correct letter.
Which of these names might be given to a child born on February 5? Write the correct letter.
In Ewe, the word gbe means “day.” Translate each of the following Ewe words into English.

hints.text: Don't look at the dates as numbers — look them up on the calendars and write the day of the week next to each name. Several different dates in the data fall on the same weekday.

Each name splits into two parts: a piece that marks the child's sex (a prefix like Kwa-/Kɔ- for boys or A- for girls) and a piece that identifies the weekday. Names for the same weekday share that second piece.

Worked example (not one of the graded items): January 20 is a Saturday and gives the female name Ami; January 27 is also a Saturday and gives the male name Kwami. So the Saturday element is -mi, with A- for a girl and Kwa- (or Kɔ-) for a boy.

explanationHtml:
Step 1: Turn dates into weekdays

The names have nothing to do with the number on the calendar — they depend on the day of the week. So the very first move is to use the two calendars and relabel every example:

DateWeekdayNameSex
Jan 7SundayKɔsiM
Jan 14SundayKwasiM
Feb 11SundayAkosuaF
Jan 15MondayKɔdzoM
Feb 26MondayAdzoaF
Jan 9TuesdayKɔblaM
Feb 13TuesdayKwamlaM
Feb 6TuesdayAblaF
Jan 24WednesdayAkuF
Jan 11ThursdayYawaF
Feb 22ThursdayYaoM
Jan 20SaturdayAmiF
Jan 27SaturdayKwamiM

Notice how tidy this is: the three Sunday names all contain si/sua, both Monday names contain dzo, all three Tuesday names contain bla/mla, and both Saturday names contain mi.

Step 2: Split each name into sex + weekday

This kind of splitting is morphology — the study of how words are built out of smaller meaningful pieces. Each Ewe day-name here = (piece meaning “boy” or “girl”) + (piece meaning the weekday):

  • Male names begin with Kwa- or Kɔ- (these are two variants of the same prefix): Kwasi, Kɔsi, Kɔdzo, Kɔbla, Kwamla, Kwami.
  • Female names begin with A- (and often end in -a): Abla, Aku, Ami, Adzoa, Akosua.
  • Thursday is the odd one out in shape: both Thursday names start with Ya-, with Yawa female and Yao male.

So the weekday elements we can extract are: Sunday -si / -sua, Monday -dzo, Tuesday -bla / -mla, Wednesday -ku, Thursday Ya-, Saturday -mi. Friday never appears in the examples — remember that, because the questions will make you fill the gap.

C1: male or female?

Just read off the prefix. Awusi and Adzo and Afiwa all start with A- means female. Kwadzo starts with Kwa- means male. Kofi doesn't have A-, and its Ko- looks just like the Kɔ- of Kɔsi, Kɔdzo, Kɔbla are all male. (Answers: F, M, F, M, F.)

C2: matching dates to names

Convert each date to a weekday, then find the name with the matching weekday element:

  • Jan 10 = Wednesday, so the Wednesday element is -ku, giving Kɔku (b).
  • Jan 13 = Saturday, so -mi, giving Kɔmi (e).
  • Jan 16 = Tuesday, so -bla, giving Abla (f).
  • Jan 26 = Friday, so the only name left that we can't tie to any other weekday is Afua (a). This is where the missing Friday slot pays off.
  • Jan 29 = Monday, so -dzo, giving Adzoa (d).
  • Feb 8 = Thursday, so Ya-, giving Yao (c).

C3 and C4: using Friday and Monday

From C1 we know Kofi is male, and neither -fi nor the female Afi/Afiwa matches any weekday we already labelled — so -fi must be the missing Friday. Of the three choices in C3, only January 12 is a Friday, so the answer is (a).

For C4, February 5 is a Monday. Monday is -dzo, so the name is Kwadzo, choice (a). (Afi would be Friday and Kwaku Wednesday.)

C5: gbe = “day”

Ewe forms the names of weekdays the same way it forms the personal names: a weekday element plus the word for “day.” In Dzoɗagbe you can see the Monday element dzo (as in Kɔdzo, Adzoa), so it means Monday. In Fiɗagbe you can see the Friday element fi (as in Kofi, Afiwa), so it means Friday. The extra ɗa is just a linking piece that shows up in all the weekday words.
